introduction: On this Sunday, Jeremiah announces that God will bring his people home, including the blind and the lame. In the Gospel, the blind beggar Bartimaeus cries out, Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. Jesus calls him, heals him, and Bartimaeus follows him on the way. The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of Christ our high priest. Let us cry out to Jesus with faith and follow him.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord has done great things for us. Let us bring him our prayers with faith.
intentions: For the Church: that she may hear the cries of the poor and bring them to Jesus. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the blind and all who live with disabilities: that they may be welcomed and helped. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are told to be quiet and stay on the side of the road: that their voices may be heard. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who cannot see their way forward: that Christ may open their eyes. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may answer the question of Jesus, What do you want me to do for you, and follow him. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus, Son of David, you heard the cry of Bartimaeus and opened his eyes. Have mercy on us, heal our blindness, and help us to follow you on the way. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: Have mercy on me
reflection.body:
Jeremiah sings of a homecoming. God will gather his scattered people "from the uttermost parts of the earth, along with the blind and the lame." No one is left behind. "I am a father to Israel," says the Lord.

In the Gospel, Jesus is leaving Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, and a blind beggar named Bartimaeus is sitting by the road. When he hears that Jesus is passing, he cries out: "Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!" The crowd tells him to be quiet. He only shouts louder.

Jesus stops. He says, "Call him." And the people who had told Bartimaeus to be silent now say, "Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!" Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, perhaps the only thing he owned, springs up and comes to Jesus.

Jesus asks him a question he asked James and John last week: "What do you want me to do for you?" They had asked for glory; Bartimaeus asks for what he really needs: "Rabboni, that I may see again." Jesus tells him, "Go your way. Your faith has made you well." But Bartimaeus does not go his own way. Mark says, "Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way" to Jerusalem and the cross.

Bartimaeus teaches us how to pray: with persistence, with honesty about what we need, and with readiness to follow. His cry for mercy to the Son of David has become one of the great prayers of the Church.

This week, pray his words often during the day. Let Jesus ask you, "What do you want me to do for you?" and answer him honestly. And notice anyone around you who is being told to be quiet, and help bring them to Jesus.
